name: boscaiola
instructions:
Pasta alla boscaiola — the traditional italian 'woodsman-style' pasta, mushroom + cream + tomato paste + onion + alcohol (brandy or white wine) + parmesan. Cream and tomato together push this into the 'rosa' / blush territory rather than strictly white (bianca) or red (rossa). Written down here with Sip and Feast's brandy-forward take as the primary scaffold — brandy is the alcohol slot that pushes the dish into french-cognac-mushroom-sauce depth territory (traditional boscaiola uses white wine; brandy is Sip and Feast's substitution and I want to try it as the default).

This recipe replaces a previous attempt to build a WHITE-SAUCE MUSHROOM ALFREDO (heavy cream OR cream cheese versions) in this file. Both alfredo directions plateaued — see FOOTNOTES at the bottom of notes for what was tried and why it didn't stick.

SERVES 4. Sip and Feast base.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 1 lb pasta (spaghetti, fettuccine, linguine, penne, or rigatoni all work — Sip and Feast's recipe is pasta-shape flexible)
- 3 tbsp olive oil (Sip and Feast — no butter). BUTTER is the alternative if you want a richer register (see notes)
- 1½ lb cremini mushrooms (baby bella), sliced ¼-inch thick. Shiitake / oyster / lions mane also work (see notes)
- 1 medium yellow onion, diced
- 4 cloves garlic, minced (my add — Sip and Feast skips it but boscaiola tradition includes garlic)
- 3 oz tomato paste
- 1 cup brandy (or 1 cup dry white wine for the more traditional boscaiola direction — see notes)
- 1¼ cups heavy cream
- 2 cups reserved pasta water (of which ~1 cup goes into the sauce, the rest for adjusting)
- ½ cup freshly grated parmigiano reggiano (NOT pre-shredded — see notes)
- ¼ cup fresh italian parsley, minced
- salt and pepper

TRADITIONAL ADDITIONS (secondary — see notes):
- Pancetta or italian sausage (cooked and rendered before the mushroom sear) — traditional in boscaiola
- Peas (1 cup frozen, added at the end) — traditional 'green' inclusion

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. BOIL SALTED WATER (2 tbsp kosher salt per gallon) for the pasta.

2. SEAR MUSHROOMS IN BATCHES: heat a large stainless steel pan to medium. Add 2 tbsp olive oil. Working in batches to avoid crowding, sauté mushrooms until browned on both sides (~6-8 min per batch). Season with salt/pepper. TRANSFER TO A PLATE, tent with foil. Pulling the mushrooms is important — lets the sauce reduce cleanly without stewing the mushrooms.

3. COOK AROMATICS: reduce heat to medium-low. Add the diced onion with additional oil if needed. Sauté until translucent (~4-5 min). Add garlic in the last 30 seconds. Stir in the 3 oz tomato paste and cook 5 min, stirring frequently — this caramelizes the tomato paste and builds real depth.

4. START PASTA: cook the spaghetti (or your chosen pasta) to one minute LESS than al dente. Reserve 2 cups pasta water before draining.

5. DEGLAZE WITH BRANDY: pour in the 1 cup brandy. Increase heat to high. Scrape up brown bits with a wooden spoon. Cook ~2 min until the alcohol smell dissipates and the liquid reduces by about half.

6. BUILD THE SAUCE: reduce heat to medium. Add 1 cup reserved pasta water; cook 2 min. Pour in the 1¼ cups heavy cream. Bring to a simmer, stirring frequently. Taste and season with salt/pepper.

7. RECOMBINE: add the seared mushrooms back to the sauce. Add the drained pasta directly to the sauce. Cook until the pasta reaches al dente, then remove from heat.

8. FINISH: stir in the ½ cup freshly grated parmigiano and ¼ cup minced fresh parsley. If the sauce is too dry, add reserved pasta water 1-2 oz at a time to loosen.
notes:
Source: Sip and Feast — Mushroom Brandy Cream Sauce Spaghetti (https://www.sipandfeast.com/mushroom-brandy-cream-sauce-spaghetti/). Written down here as the primary scaffold for what's really a boscaiola build. See FOOTNOTES at the bottom for the prior mushroom-alfredo attempts this file replaces.

=== WHAT BOSCAIOLA IS (WOODSMAN-STYLE PASTA) ===

Pasta alla boscaiola ('woodsman-style') is a traditional italian pasta with mushrooms as the signature ingredient (from bosco = forest). Three main forms:

- BIANCA (WHITE): cream + mushrooms + onion + white wine + parmesan. No tomato.
- ROSSA (RED): tomato + mushrooms + sausage/pancetta + wine. No cream.
- ROSA / BLUSH: both cream AND tomato (usually tomato paste rather than crushed). This recipe.

Common traditional inclusions: pancetta or italian sausage, peas, parsley to finish, white wine deglaze, parmigiano or pecorino.

Sip and Feast's version is a rosa/blush boscaiola with brandy substituted for the traditional white wine — a distinctly non-traditional move that pushes the alcohol slot from italian-fresh-wine into french-caramel-cognac territory. That substitution is the reason this recipe is worth trying: brandy adds richer, more caramel-fruit depth than white wine does.

=== BRANDY vs WHITE WINE (SIP AND FEAST'S SUBSTITUTION) ===

Sip and Feast uses 1 cup brandy where traditional boscaiola uses ~½ cup white wine. Brandy has:
- Higher alcohol content (~40% vs ~12% for wine) — needs longer reduction to drive off
- Caramel + fruit + oak flavor character from barrel-aging (wine reads bright + grape)
- French cognac-mushroom-sauce tradition backing (classical french mushroom sauces routinely use cognac)

BOTH ARE VALID — brandy pushes richer/deeper, white wine keeps it more traditionally italian-fresh. Sip and Feast's swap is the going-forward default here, but note white wine is the historical boscaiola alcohol.

=== PANCETTA / ITALIAN SAUSAGE (TRADITIONAL, SECONDARY) ===

Traditional boscaiola almost always includes pancetta or italian sausage — the meat/fat is what makes it a 'woodsman' dish (hearty, sticks-to-your-ribs). Sip and Feast's version is vegetarian; adding pancetta (diced, rendered before the mushroom sear) or italian sausage (crumbled, cooked before the mushroom sear) would push this recipe into a more traditional register.

=== PEAS (TRADITIONAL, SECONDARY — THE 'GREEN' INCLUSION) ===

One cup of frozen peas stirred in near the end (with the mushrooms) is very traditional and adds visual contrast + sweetness. Sip and Feast skips them; adding is fine and traditional.

=== MUSHROOM CHOICE — CREMINI TRADITIONAL; SHIITAKE / OYSTER / LIONS MANE UPGRADES ===

Sip and Feast uses cremini (baby bella) mushrooms — traditional boscaiola choice, widely available, holds up well against the tomato + cream + brandy sauce.

OTHER MUSHROOM OPTIONS from earlier experiments in this file's history:
- SHIITAKE or OYSTER: work well; more distinctive mushroom flavor than cremini. Would push the dish slightly more assertive.
- LIONS MANE: the celebratory pick. Denser, meatier, more distinctive. Right for occasions.
- PORTABELLA: works, deeper meatier flavor. Would tilt the dish more assertively mushroomy.
- WHITE BUTTON: higher water content, less depth. Cremini is a better default.

Mix + match is fine. Cremini is the default; the others are upgrades.

=== PAN-FRIED MUSHROOMS ARE STILL LOAD-BEARING ===

Carrying over from the alfredo iterations — the mushroom sear is where the mushroom flavor lives. Don't shortcut this step.
- DON'T WASH THEM: damp cloth. Water adds moisture and steams the fry.
- SPACE THEM OUT (SEAR IN BATCHES): don't cram; they'll steam not fry.
- DON'T SALT AT THE START: draws out moisture. Season AFTER golden.
- PULL THEM OUT after searing: lets the sauce reduce without them stewing (Sip and Feast's technique — a real improvement over keeping them in the pan the whole time).

=== FRESHLY GRATED PARMIGIANO — NOT PRE-SHREDDED ===

Use freshly grated parmigiano reggiano. Pre-shredded packet cheese doesn't melt properly — anti-caking additives mess with sauce texture. Microplane or box grater.

NO GRUYÈRE HERE — that was an alfredo iteration move. Traditional boscaiola uses parmigiano or pecorino, one cheese, at the finishing stage.

=== OLIVE OIL vs BUTTER ===

Sip and Feast uses only olive oil. Prior alfredo iterations landed on butter as the fat. Both are legitimate:
- OLIVE OIL: cleaner, brighter, lets the mushroom + brandy + tomato paste flavors lead. Sip and Feast's default.
- BUTTER: richer, adds a dairy dimension the sauce doesn't otherwise have. Would push the dish more decadent.

Start with olive oil per Sip and Feast; try butter as an experiment if the sauce reads under-fatted.

=== FOOTNOTE 1 — HEAVY CREAM MUSHROOM ALFREDO ATTEMPT (BORING — WHY BOSCAIOLA WON) ===

Standard mushroom alfredo (butter + heavy cream + mushrooms + parmesan + pasta water) is the obvious starting point for creamy-mushroom-pasta and I've tried variations of it. It's BORING. The cream just enriches without contributing dimension; the parmesan and butter are doing all the flavor work; mushrooms add texture more than they add depth. The whole dish reads one-note-creamy.

Why boscaiola wins here: the flavor architecture — mushroom sear + ONION SWEETNESS + TOMATO PASTE CARAMELIZATION + BRANDY CARAMEL/FRUIT + cream + parmesan — covers the same 'creamy mushroom pasta' territory with real dimension. The tomato paste + onion + brandy trio is what the heavy cream alfredo is missing. Without them, cream + mushrooms is just a sauce that happens to have mushrooms in it.

=== FOOTNOTE 2 — CREAM CHEESE MUSHROOM ALFREDO ATTEMPT (TECHNIQUE ADVANCE, RECIPE PLATEAU) ===

Prior version of this file — Chris Collins' Don't Go Bacon My Heart recipe (mushroom tagliatelle) with cream cheese as the sauce body, refined over multiple cooks. Reached 'has potential' but didn't advance to 'excellent.' Documented here as a real experiment worth remembering.

WHAT WAS BUILT:
- Cream cheese pre-loosened with CHICKEN STOCK + POTATO STARCH before hitting the pan — prevents cream-cheese blobs, sauce integrates cleanly, starch stabilizes against acid. Real technique advance for cream cheese sauces in general (transferable to other applications).
- BUTTER (not olive oil) as the fat.
- SUNFLOWER SEEDS toasted with the garlic in the middle of the pan (~1-2 min sauté after mushrooms pushed aside) — adds toasty texture. Novel move.
- WHITE WINE deglaze on the mushrooms.
- GRUYÈRE alongside parmesan at the finishing stage (double cheese).
- BASIL chiffonaded at the end.
- SHIITAKE or OYSTER preferred, LIONS MANE celebratory.
- Tagliatelle or fettuccine (walked back the 'tagliatelle only' rule).

WHAT DIDN'T STICK / WHY IT PLATEAUED:
- Solid but not exciting. The sauce had body and technique but was missing DIMENSION — the flavor stack was cream cheese + mushroom + wine + parmesan/gruyère, which is a lot of dairy weight and not much else.
- Adding porcini powder, red chili flakes, or other seasonings didn't fix it (walked back — they crowded rather than added).
- Fennel powder was actively bad (clashing).
- The core issue: NO SWEETNESS LAYER (no onion, no tomato paste caramelization), NO ASSERTIVE ALCOHOL (white wine is too mild here), NO GREEN/BRIGHT (basil chiffonade helped but wasn't enough).

WHY BOSCAIOLA IS THE RIGHT NEXT MOVE:
- The cream cheese + starch + stock technique is a valid tool but this dish doesn't need it — heavy cream in a properly-built sauce (with onion + tomato paste + brandy providing structure) has enough body.
- The missing dimensions in the alfredo attempt (sweetness, tomato caramelization, assertive alcohol) are exactly what boscaiola provides.
- The cream cheese + stock + starch technique is preserved as a skill for other applications; not the right tool for this dish.

TECHNIQUES WORTH TRYING FROM THE ALFREDO WORK IN THIS BOSCAIOLA CONTEXT:
- Sunflower seeds toasted with the garlic (step 3 here — add them with the garlic in the last 30 seconds) — might add nice texture. Untested in boscaiola context.
- Butter instead of olive oil for the fat (variation — see OLIVE OIL vs BUTTER note above).
- Fresh basil at the end (in addition to or instead of parsley) — untested in boscaiola context.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- italian-tomato-sauces: the strictly-tomato italian pasta sauce family. This recipe's rosa/blush character (cream + tomato paste together) sits between italian-tomato-sauces and a pure cream sauce.
- spinach-ricotta: uses cream cheese in a different application. The pre-loosen-with-stock-and-starch technique developed in the alfredo footnote could transfer here if that recipe needs body work in the future.
